title: Bilal, the Voice That Would Not Break
period: Dawn of Islam, Mecca and Medina
teaser: Under a heavy rock on the open sand, a man is ordered to give up his faith; tradition relates he answers with a single word. Where would that voice be heard next?
story:
Noon in the valley of Mecca, under a merciless sun. According to the traditional accounts, a man is made to lie on the open sand with a heavy rock on his chest, while his master Umayya ibn Khalaf demands one thing: that he give up his new faith. Tradition relates that Bilal answered with a single word, repeated again and again: Ahad, Ahad — One, One.

Bilal ibn Rabah was a slave of Abyssinian origin, and one of the very first people in Mecca to accept Islam. That made his position terribly exposed. A free man from a strong clan could count on his relatives to speak up for him. Bilal had no clan, no wealth, no rank, and nobody in the city bound to defend him. Umayya, one of the leading men of Quraysh and an opponent of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, could do as he liked. All Bilal had was his conviction, and it proved stronger than the stone.

The early sources relate that the torment ended when Abu Bakr, a close companion of the Prophet ﷺ, bought him and set him free. The hardest years of the small Muslim community were still ahead of them, and in 622 they left Mecca for Medina.

In Medina the community was growing, and a question became pressing: how should people be summoned to prayer? The early sources relate that several ideas were discussed. In the end the Prophet ﷺ chose Bilal, whose voice carried far. It is reported that he gave the call from a rooftop near the mosque. The man who had once been forced into silence under a rock became the first muezzin of Islam.

Then came the year 630. The Muslims entered Mecca, and the early biographies relate that Bilal gave the call to prayer from the top of the Kaaba. It was the same city where he had been tortured. Now his voice rose above its rooftops and over the valley where he had once lain helpless in the heat.

After the Prophet's death, Bilal went to Syria, where he died around the year 640. Fourteen centuries later, the call he was the first to raise still rises five times a day all over the world.
lesson: A person's worth does not come from origin, wealth or status, but from what they stand for. Hold on to what you know is true, even when you seem to stand alone.

title: Al-Khwarizmi and the Book That Named Algebra
teaser: The book that gave us the word algebra contains no x, no plus sign and no equals sign. How did al-Khwarizmi solve problems in words alone, and why does his name still echo in our computers?
story:
Baghdad, around the year 820. A scholar sits down to write a book for a very practical reason. In the markets, the courts and the surveyors' offices, people keep running into the same kind of problem: a legacy must be shared among heirs, a field must be measured, a canal must be dug, a trade account must be settled. Each time, something is unknown, and each time it must be found.

The scholar is Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, and his name points to Khwarazm, a region of Central Asia south of the Aral Sea. He works in the time of the caliph al-Ma'mun, who ruled from 813 to 833 and was a great patron of learning. Later tradition links him to the House of Wisdom, the circle of scholars gathered in the capital.

His book is called, in short, the Book of Completion and Balancing. One of its operations is al-jabr, which means restoring or completing: if a quantity is missing on one side of a problem, you put it back on both. From that word comes our word algebra. The book sorts problems into a small number of standard types and gives a method for each. One famous example asks for a square which, together with ten of its own roots, makes thirty-nine. The answer is a root of three, and a square of nine.

Here is the surprise. The book has no symbols at all: no x, no equals sign, no plus. Everything is written out in words, in full sentences. To show why a method works, al-Khwarizmi draws squares and rectangles and completes them into a larger square, so that the reader can see the answer with their own eyes. A large part of the book is given to inheritance problems, which shows how closely it was tied to everyday life.

In the twelfth century the book was translated into Latin, and European scholars learned from it for generations. Another of his works explained the Indian way of writing numbers with nine digits and a zero. Its original Arabic text has not survived, but a Latin version begins with the words Dixit Algorizmi, Algorizmi has said. In Latin his name became Algoritmi, which gave us the word algorithm.

His greatest legacy is a way of thinking: break a problem into steps, and write them down so clearly that anyone can follow. Each time a phone or a computer runs a program, it echoes the name of a scholar from Baghdad.
lesson: The most lasting knowledge often begins with a wish to be useful. Explain things clearly, step by step, and your work can serve people you will never meet.

title: Fatima al-Fihri and the Mosque of al-Qarawiyyin
teaser: According to the chroniclers, a merchant's daughter inherits a fortune and decides to give all of it away to build a mosque. What do we really know about her, and what grew from that gift?
story:
Fez, in the middle of the ninth century. According to the chroniclers, a woman has just inherited a fortune from her father, a merchant. She could spend it on a comfortable life. Instead, tradition relates, she decides to give all of it to build a mosque for her community.

The city she lives in is young. Fez had been founded only a few decades earlier by the Idrisid rulers, and it was growing fast. A river ran through the valley and divided it into two shores. For a community of newcomers, a mosque was far more than a place of prayer. It was a meeting place, a shaded refuge in summer and a centre around which a neighbourhood could organise its life. On one side lived families who had come from al-Andalus; on the other, migrants from Kairouan, in present-day Tunisia, who gave their name to their quarter.

Her name is Fatima al-Fihri. According to the Moroccan chroniclers, her family belonged to that community from Kairouan. The mosque she is said to have founded, in the year 859, took the name of the quarter: al-Qarawiyyin, the mosque of the people of Kairouan. The same accounts say that she fasted until the building was finished, and that her sister Maryam founded another mosque across the river, the mosque of the Andalusians.

What we know of Fatima comes from accounts written several centuries later, and historians treat the details with caution. That is worth saying plainly. We cannot be sure of every word the chroniclers tell. But the building is very real.

Over the following centuries, one dynasty after another enlarged it, until it became a vast mosque with many aisles. Around its prayer hall, teachers gathered students, and al-Qarawiyyin became one of the great centres of learning of the Muslim world. Students came to study law, grammar, mathematics and astronomy, and the mosque gained a famous library. The old city of Fez, with al-Qarawiyyin at its heart, is today a World Heritage Site.

A gift of this kind is the sort of lasting charity that Muslims have always valued: its benefit goes on for as long as people use it. Here, it has lasted for more than eleven centuries. It is often described as the oldest university in the world still in operation, born from one woman's decision to turn an inheritance into a gift.
lesson: What you keep for yourself ends with you; what you give to learning can outlive you by a thousand years. Ask what your means, large or small, could build for others.

title: Ibn Battuta: He Left for Mecca and Kept Going
period: Marinid Morocco and the wider Muslim world
teaser: In June 1325 a young man of twenty-one rode out of Tangier, saying he left alone, to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. He would not come home for good for nearly thirty years: where did the road take him?
story:
In June 1325, a young man of twenty-one rides out of Tangier, in Morocco. He writes later that he left alone, with no companion and no caravan, sad to leave his parents. His plan is simple: to perform the pilgrimage to Mecca. He will not come home for good for nearly thirty years.

His name is Ibn Battuta. He crosses North Africa, reaches Egypt and Damascus, and joins the pilgrims on the long desert road to Mecca, a journey of weeks. Many young men would have gone home after the pilgrimage. He did not. He comes back to Mecca more than once, but curiosity carries him further and further: Iraq and Persia, the coast of East Africa, Anatolia, the steppes of Central Asia.

He crosses the mountains into India, where the sultan of Delhi makes him a judge. Trained in Islamic law, he finds that this training opens doors almost everywhere: a mosque, fellow scholars and a welcome. Sent by the sultan as an envoy toward China, he suffers a shipwreck off the coast of India and loses nearly everything. He serves as a judge again in the Maldives, and his account takes him as far as China, though historians debate some stages of the route.

He is back in the Middle East in 1348, and he writes that he was in Damascus when the Black Death struck. Plague was then sweeping through much of the known world. Soon afterwards he returns to Morocco. And still he is not finished. On his last great journey, he crosses the Sahara to visit the empire of Mali. He reports that the houses at the salt mines of Taghaza were built of blocks of salt, and in Mali he praises the safety of the roads, though some local customs surprise him.

In all, he is thought to have covered about 120,000 kilometres, probably more than any other traveller known before modern times.

Back in Morocco, the sultan asks him to dictate his memories to a writer named Ibn Juzayy. The book, known as the Rihla, the Journey, from its long title A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Travelling, was finished around 1355. It remains one of our best windows onto the fourteenth-century world, with its markets, courts, roads and people.
lesson: A first step taken with a sincere purpose can lead much further than you imagined. Stay curious about people who live differently from you, and write down what you learn.

title: Cordoba: A Forest of Columns
teaser: Hundreds of columns carry double arches striped in red and white, row after row, in a hall whose aisles seem endless. It began with a refugee prince: why did his builders stack one arch upon another?
story:
Step inside, and you seem to enter a forest of stone: hundreds of columns, row after row, carrying double arches striped in red and white. The light is dim and the aisles seem to have no end. This is the Great Mosque of Cordoba, in southern Spain.

It begins with a refugee. Abd al-Rahman I was an Umayyad prince who had fled Syria as a young man, after his family lost power in 750. He crossed North Africa and founded a new state in al-Andalus, with Cordoba as its capital. Around 785 he began a mosque there. Later accounts relate that he bought from the city's Christians the church site they shared with the Muslims.

His builders faced a problem. They reused columns taken from older Roman and Visigothic buildings, and these were short. A low ceiling would have made a cramped hall. So they placed a second arch above the first, raising the roof, and alternated brick and stone in red and white. A practical solution became the building's signature.

Over two centuries, as Cordoba grew into one of the largest cities in Europe, his successors enlarged the mosque again and again. In the tenth century the caliph al-Hakam II enlarged the prayer hall and added a magnificent mihrab, the niche showing the direction of prayer. Its gold mosaics were made with the help of craftsmen who, according to the sources, were sent from Byzantium. Near the end of that century the powerful minister al-Mansur, known in the Christian chronicles as Almanzor, added the last great extension, widening the hall toward the east. Columns and arches simply continued, row after row.

In 1236 Cordoba was taken by the king of Castile, and the mosque became a cathedral. In the sixteenth century, from 1523, a church nave was built in its centre. The building survived the change of faith, and the forest of arches still stands around it.

Today the monument is a World Heritage Site, and people come from all over the world to walk through its aisles. Its story is the story of a prince in exile who built something so well that centuries, kings and religions could not make it disappear.
lesson: A limit can become a signature: the builders' short columns produced their most beautiful idea. When your means fall short, look for the clever solution instead of giving up.

title: Ibn Sina and the Canon of Medicine
period: Samanid Central Asia and Buyid Persia
teaser: At sixteen he was already treating patients; at about eighteen he was called to a ruler's bedside and gained what he wanted most, the royal library. What did that young reader go on to write?
story:
At sixteen he was already treating patients. At about eighteen he was called to the bedside of the ruler of Bukhara, and what he gained from it was the thing he wanted most: permission to use the royal library.

This is how Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, tells his own youth in his autobiography. Born around 980 near Bukhara, in present-day Uzbekistan, the capital of the Samanid state and a city famous for its scholars, he says he had memorised the Qur'an by the age of ten. He also tells how he struggled with the Metaphysics of Aristotle, reading it many times without understanding, until a short commentary by the philosopher al-Farabi, which he found in a bookseller's stall, finally made it clear.

The library was a treasure house. He describes rooms full of chests of books, each room devoted to a different subject. He read what he could find. Some time later, he reports, the library burned down, and some people said he had set the fire to keep its contents to himself.

His adult life was far from calm. When the Samanid dynasty fell around the end of the tenth century, he left Bukhara. He moved from court to court across Persia, serving as physician and sometimes as minister, writing wherever he stopped. He wrote a vast philosophical encyclopedia, the Book of Healing, and another great work that would carry his name across the world.

That work is the Canon of Medicine. In five books, it organises the medical knowledge of his time: the principles of medicine, simple remedies, diseases of each part of the body, illnesses that affect the whole body such as fevers, and compound medicines. Its strength was its order: a doctor could find what he needed. It even lays down rules for testing a new remedy, such as trying it on a single, uncomplicated illness, so that its effect could be judged fairly.

Translated into Latin in the twelfth century, the Canon was taught in European universities for centuries, in some places until the seventeenth century. Ibn Sina died in 1037 in Hamadan, in Iran, at about fifty-seven, after an illness. His tomb there is still visited.
lesson: Knowledge becomes useful to others when it is put in order. Read widely while you are young, then take the trouble to organise what you know so that others can use it.

title: Mansa Musa, the Pilgrim King of Mali
teaser: In 1324 a caravan arrived in Cairo so rich that the city talked about it for years, and gold lost value there. Who rode at its head, and what did he bring home?
story:
Cairo, 1324. A caravan arrives from across the Sahara, so rich that the city will talk about it for years. At its head rides Musa, the mansa — the king — of Mali, on his way to Mecca for the pilgrimage. Cairo was then one of the largest and busiest cities of the Muslim world, and its people were not easily impressed.

Behind him lay a long road, and ahead of him a very different world. His empire, in West Africa, grew rich from the gold trade, and its trade routes crossed the Sahara, where caravans carried gold north and salt south. To reach Egypt, Musa and his companions had to cross the desert itself, a journey of months through heat and sand.

In Cairo, which was then ruled by the Mamluk sultans, and where the gold of West Africa was well known to merchants, Musa and his companions gave away and spent so much gold that the metal lost value there. The scholar al-Umari, who visited the city about twelve years later, wrote that its price had still not recovered. The exact size of the caravan is unknown; the figures given by later writers are impossible to verify. But the accounts agree on the impression it made.

Musa continued to Mecca, performed the pilgrimage, and made the long return journey. Chroniclers relate that by then his funds had run low, and that he borrowed from merchants in Cairo and repaid them generously. He brought back more than fame. He returned with scholars and books, and with an Andalusian poet, Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, whom tradition remembers as an architect and credits with the great Djinguereber mosque of Timbuktu, a city that would become a famous centre of learning.

News of the journey travelled far. In 1375, a map drawn in Majorca, the Catalan Atlas, showed the king of Mali seated on a throne, holding a nugget of gold. Traders and mapmakers in the Mediterranean, who had never crossed the Sahara, now knew of a great kingdom to the south.

A pilgrimage had put West Africa on the map of the world. Musa is remembered as a king whose faith and generosity linked Mali to Cairo, Mecca and the Mediterranean.
lesson: Wealth is remembered for what it built, not for how brightly it shone. Whatever you gain, invest part of it in knowledge and in things that will serve others.

title: Baghdad and the House of Wisdom
teaser: In ninth-century Baghdad a Christian physician, a Muslim mathematician and a Sabian astronomer could be found bent over the same books. What brought them together, and how far did their work travel?
story:
In ninth-century Baghdad, a Christian physician, a Muslim mathematician and a Sabian astronomer from Harran could find themselves bent over the same books. What brought them together was one of the great efforts of human history: translating the knowledge of the ancient world into Arabic.

The city itself was new. Baghdad had been founded in 762 by the caliph al-Mansur, and it quickly became a crossroads of languages and peoples. The Abbasid caliphs, especially al-Ma'mun, who ruled from 813 to 833, supported the translation movement. At their court stood the Bayt al-Hikma, the House of Wisdom. Historians debate exactly what it was, probably a royal library where scholars and copyists worked, and the translation movement was much wider, paid for by many patrons. But the name has come to stand for the whole adventure.

Manuscripts were hunted down. Works of Greek medicine, mathematics, astronomy and philosophy, along with Persian and Indian texts, were sought out, sometimes far away, and bought for the translators. Wealthy families, among them the three brothers known as the Banu Musa, sponsored translators and sent agents in search of rare books. Euclid's Elements was translated more than once, and Ptolemy's great book on astronomy came into Arabic as al-Majisti, which is how Europe later came to call it the Almagest.

The work demanded great care. Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Christian from Iraq, translated a large part of the works of the physician Galen. He explained that he compared several manuscripts to establish a reliable text before translating it. Thabit ibn Qurra, a Sabian from Harran, worked on mathematics and astronomy. Many translators worked through Syriac, the language of Eastern Christian scholars, as well as directly from Greek.

Scholars did not only translate: they checked, corrected and went further. Al-Khwarizmi wrote his algebra in this Baghdad. Astronomers set up observatories in Baghdad and Damascus and measured the sky themselves. Mathematicians invented new methods, and physicians tested what the Greeks had written against their own experience.

Centuries later, much of this knowledge reached Europe through Latin translations made from Arabic. A chain of translators, from Greek to Syriac to Arabic to Latin, had carried the heritage of the ancient world across the centuries.
lesson: Knowledge grows when people are humble enough to learn from those who came before, whatever their origin. Take the best of what others have found, check it, and add your own part.

title: How Paper Changed the World of Books
teaser: A sheet of paper seems like nothing, yet when it reached the Muslim world in the eighth century it changed how knowledge was kept. Did Chinese prisoners really teach the craft in Samarkand?
story:
A sheet of paper seems like nothing. Yet when it reached the Muslim world, in the eighth century, it changed how knowledge was kept and shared.

Paper had been invented in China many centuries earlier, traditionally credited to a court official named Cai Lun around the year 105. A famous account, written down long afterwards, says that Chinese prisoners taken at the battle of Talas, in Central Asia, in 751, taught the craft in Samarkand. Historians doubt that it happened so simply: paper was probably already known in the region. What is certain is that Samarkand became famous for its paper, made from linen and hemp rags.

Egyptian papyrus, made from a reed of the Nile, had served for thousands of years, but it grew mainly in Egypt. Now imagine the process. Old rags were soaked and beaten into a pulp. A worker dipped a fine mould into the pulp and lifted out a thin layer of fibres, which was pressed and dried into a sheet. It was cheap, light and smooth. It was also hard to scrape clean without leaving a trace, which is often noted as an advantage for official records.

From Samarkand the craft travelled west. By about 800, paper was being made in Baghdad, and the Abbasid administration adopted it for its records. Paper was cheaper than parchment, which was made from animal skins, and easier to obtain than Egyptian papyrus. A single parchment book could take the skins of many animals; paper let a copyist produce books at a far lower cost.

The effect was enormous. Books multiplied; Baghdad had a whole market of booksellers and copyists; great libraries appeared. Scholars could own more books, and students could take notes. A bookseller of Baghdad, Ibn al-Nadim, compiled around 987 a great catalogue of the books of his time, the Fihrist, which gives some idea of how rich the world of books had become. Writing was no longer reserved for the very rich.

Papermaking then spread to Syria, Egypt, North Africa and al-Andalus, where the town of Xàtiva was known for its paper by the twelfth century. From Spain and Italy it later spread across the rest of Europe, long before printing arrived.
lesson: A humble tool can change more lives than a famous monument. Never look down on what is simple and cheap if it helps knowledge reach more people.

title: How the Qur'an Was Gathered Into One Book
teaser: About 633, after a battle in which many who knew the Qur'an by heart were killed, Umar went to the caliph fearing that part of the revelation could be lost. What did they decide to do?
story:
The year is about 633. At the battle of Yamama, many of those who knew the Qur'an by heart have just been killed. Umar ibn al-Khattab is worried and goes to the caliph Abu Bakr: if more memorisers die, part of the revelation could be lost. He urges him to gather the whole Qur'an in writing.

The Qur'an was already written down. During the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, scribes had recorded the revelation on whatever was at hand, and many Companions knew it by heart. But it had not been gathered between two covers, and the danger now seemed real.

Abu Bakr hesitates at first: how could he do something the Prophet ﷺ had not done? Then he is convinced. The caliph has other worries too: he leads a young community through a time of crisis. He entrusts the task to a young man, Zayd ibn Thabit, who had been one of the Prophet's scribes. Zayd later said that moving a mountain would have seemed lighter to him. He collected the text from pieces of parchment, palm stalks, flat stones, animal shoulder bones and the memories of men. It is reported that he accepted nothing unless it was confirmed in writing and by witnesses. The finished sheets were kept by Abu Bakr, then by Umar, then by Umar's daughter Hafsa.

Some years later, under the caliph Uthman, Muslims lived from Egypt to Persia. A Companion named Hudhayfa returned from a campaign alarmed: people were disputing over how to recite. The Muslims were now spread across a vast territory, far from Medina, and he feared that such differences would only grow with distance.

Uthman acted. He had a group led by Zayd make copies from Hafsa's sheets, and sent them to the great cities, with the sheets returned to Hafsa afterwards. Copies went to cities such as Basra, Kufa and Damascus, and one was kept in Medina. Each served as a reference, so that Muslims everywhere could rely on the same written text.

The Qur'an that Muslims read all over the world today follows the written text of those copies. A worry voiced in a time of grief became a work of care, handed from one generation of readers to the next.
lesson: What is precious must be protected before it is in danger, not after. Listen to the person who warns you early, and do carefully the work that others will rely on.

title: Ibn al-Bawwab, the Doorkeeper's Son
period: Abbasid Caliphate under the Buyids, Baghdad
teaser: He was a doorkeeper's son who began, it is said, by painting walls, and became the most admired calligrapher of his age. How did a reed pen lift him so high?
story:
His name means the doorkeeper's son, and that is exactly what he was: the child of a man who guarded a door in Baghdad. He began, it is said, as a house decorator, painting walls and patterns. He became the most admired calligrapher of his age.

Think of what that meant. In the Baghdad of his day, a good hand was a path to prestige. Letters, official documents, poems and Qur'ans all had to be written by someone, and the best scribes were known by name. Ibn al-Bawwab lived around the year 1000 and died there around 1022. Baghdad was then governed by the Buyid emirs, while the Abbasid caliph remained its nominal head, and the city's courts and libraries still needed fine scribes. He did not come from a family of scholars or officials. He came from the door, and he rose on the strength of his pen.

He stood on the shoulders of a predecessor. A century before him, the vizier Ibn Muqla is credited with rules giving each Arabic letter fixed proportions, measured in dots made by the pen. The idea was simple and powerful: a letter should not depend on a scribe's mood, but on measure. Ibn al-Bawwab took up this proportioned writing and gave the rounded scripts a new elegance and regularity. Such scripts had mostly been used for letters and ordinary books; in his time they came to be used for copies of the Qur'an as well.

He is said to have copied the Qur'an sixty-four times. Only one of those copies is known today: a small volume written on paper in Baghdad in the year 391 of the Hijra, 1000–1001, now kept in the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin. Its pages are decorated with gold and colour. But what strikes the eye first is the writing itself: its lines are so even that they look effortless.

Effortless is the word that hides the work. The tool was a reed pen, cut at an angle and dipped in dark ink. A line like that comes only from years of repeating the same strokes until the hand knows them. A poem on the art of writing is attributed to him, in which he describes the craft of the scribe.

Generations of calligraphers, from Iraq to Turkey, learned by imitating his style. Clear, well-proportioned Arabic writing owes much to the doorkeeper's son.
lesson: Excellence is not inherited; it is built with patient practice. Whatever your craft, the care you put into small strokes is what makes the whole page beautiful.

title: Ibn al-Haytham and the Dark Room
teaser: For centuries great minds believed we see because our eyes send out rays. In Cairo, about a thousand years ago, one man set out to test that idea in a darkened room: what did he find?
story:
For centuries, many of the greatest minds believed that we see because our eyes send out rays that touch the objects around us. It was an old and respected idea, defended by famous authorities. In Cairo, about a thousand years ago, a man set out to test that idea, and overturned it.

Al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham was born in Basra, in Iraq, around 965. Medieval biographers relate that he was invited to Egypt to regulate the floods of the Nile, realised the project was impossible, and pretended to be mad to escape the anger of the ruler. The same accounts say that he lived for years in confinement, until the ruler's death. Whatever the truth of that story, it was in Cairo that he wrote his masterpiece, the Book of Optics, in seven volumes, completed around 1021.

His method was new. He did not simply reason: he experimented. In a darkened room, he let light enter through a small hole and studied how it travelled in straight lines, forming an upside-down image on the opposite wall. He built simple devices to check his claims: a tube, a screen, a lamp. And he noticed everyday facts that the old theory could not explain. Look at the sun, and your eyes hurt. Stare at a bright light and close your eyes, and you still see its shape. How could the eye be hurt by something it was merely sending out?

He showed that vision happens when light, coming from objects, enters the eye, and not the other way round. He studied how light bends when it passes from air to water, how mirrors form images, and how the eye is built. He insisted that claims be checked by testing, and he set out a patient way of working: observe, doubt, test, and only then conclude. He even wrote that a seeker of truth should be suspicious of his own thinking as well as that of the ancients.

Translated into Latin around the year 1200, his book was studied in Europe for centuries, and scholars such as Roger Bacon and Kepler built on it. The Latin name given to him there was Alhazen.

The word camera itself recalls a dark room: camera obscura, in Latin. A single beam of light in a closed room can still show how much a patient mind can learn.
lesson: Do not accept an idea just because it is old or because famous people held it. Test it, and be ready to change your mind when the evidence asks you to.

title: Aisha, the Teacher of Medina
teaser: When the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ were unsure what he had said or done, they often knew where to go: to Aisha. What made her home in Medina a place of learning for more than forty years?
story:
In Medina, when the Companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ were unsure about what he had said or done, they often knew where to go. They went to ask Aisha.

Aisha bint Abi Bakr, wife of the Prophet ﷺ and daughter of his closest friend, had lived at his side and observed his daily life: how he prayed, how he fasted, how he behaved at home. Her room stood beside the mosque of Medina. When the Prophet ﷺ died in 632, he died in her home and was buried there. She had a sharp mind and an excellent memory, and she asked questions when she did not understand. The wives of the Prophet ﷺ are honoured by Muslims as the Mothers of the Believers, and her home was a place people approached with respect.

She was left with a great responsibility. After his death she lived for more than four decades, and her home became a place of learning. Men and women came to question her, and the early sources say that those who were not her relatives put their questions to her from behind a curtain. As the Muslim lands grew, travellers came to Medina from distant provinces looking for those who had known the Prophet ﷺ. More than two thousand hadith are transmitted on her authority, which places her among the few Companions who narrated the most. She did not only repeat: she explained, and she corrected others when she judged that they had misunderstood or misremembered. A scholar of the fourteenth century, al-Zarkashi, even gathered her corrections of other Companions into a book.

She taught the young. Her nephews Urwa ibn al-Zubayr and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad learned from her, and so did a woman scholar, Amra bint Abd al-Rahman, who was among her closest students. All three became leading teachers of the next generation, and much of what she knew passed through them.

Urwa is reported to have said that he had seen no one more learned than her in law, medicine and poetry.

She died in Medina around 678, and was buried in the cemetery of al-Baqi. A room beside the Prophet's mosque, a curtain, a stream of questions and a patient answer: such were the modest means by which one woman helped carry the knowledge of one generation to the next.
lesson: Pay attention, ask questions, and remember: what you learn carefully today, you may be the one to teach tomorrow. Sharing knowledge accurately is one of the greatest services to others.

title: Zheng He, the Admiral From Yunnan
teaser: In 1405 a fleet of enormous ships carrying about 27,000 men left the mouth of the Yangtze under a Muslim admiral from Yunnan. How did a captured boy come to command it?
story:
In 1405, a fleet leaves the mouth of the Yangtze: dozens of enormous ships and many smaller ones, carrying about 27,000 men. Sails fill the horizon. Its admiral is a Muslim from the far south-west of China. The fleet will be away for about two years.

He was born around 1371 in Yunnan, with the name Ma He. His father and grandfather both bore the title hajji, which suggests that they had made the pilgrimage to Mecca. Then came war: the armies of the Ming dynasty conquered Yunnan, and the boy was captured, made a court servant, and placed in the household of a prince. He grew into a trusted officer. When the prince became the Yongle emperor, he gave him a new name, Zheng He, and later command of the imperial fleet.

Between 1405 and 1433, Zheng He led seven great voyages across the Indian Ocean: to Java and Sumatra, to India, where the first voyage reached Calicut, a great market for pepper on the south-west coast, to Hormuz in the Gulf, to Arabia and down the coast of East Africa. The fleets carried silk and porcelain, and brought back envoys, spices and even a giraffe. The fleets sailed with the monsoon winds, calling at ports such as Malacca, Calicut and Hormuz. The largest vessels, the treasure ships, were far bigger than any ship sailing from Europe in those years, though historians debate their exact size. They were floating embassies as much as merchant vessels, carrying gifts and messages from the emperor to the rulers of the ports they visited.

The Muslim world was not unfamiliar territory for him. Among those who sailed with the fleet was Ma Huan, a Muslim who knew Arabic and served as an interpreter. He wrote an account of the lands they visited. During the last voyage, some of his companions travelled to Mecca.

His fleets carried soldiers and on occasion fought, but the main purpose of the voyages was diplomacy and trade, and the emperor wished to see the rulers of faraway lands send tribute and envoys.

He died around 1433. After his last voyage the great expeditions came to an end, and the Ming turned its attention elsewhere. His voyages had linked China to the Muslim ports of the Indian Ocean decades before European ships reached those waters.
lesson: A hard beginning does not decide where a life will end. Do faithfully the work in front of you, and you may be trusted with far greater things.

title: Al-Zahrawi, the Surgeon of Cordoba
teaser: Open the last part of a tenth-century encyclopedia and you find about two hundred drawings of surgical instruments, each one explained. Who drew them, and why did he warn that a surgeon must never act out of greed?
story:
Open the last part of his encyclopedia and you find something remarkable: drawings of surgical instruments, about two hundred of them. Scalpels, forceps, hooks, probes, cauterising irons, each one explained.

Their author, Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, lived near Cordoba in the tenth century, when al-Andalus was at its height. His name comes from Madinat al-Zahra, the palace city built by the caliphs outside Cordoba. Europe would later call him Albucasis. The palace city, begun in 936, was then in its splendour. Al-Zahrawi is generally thought to have served at the court, and to have died around the year 1013.

After nearly fifty years of practice, he gathered everything he knew into a work in thirty parts, the Kitab al-Tasrif, completed around the year 1000. He wrote it, he explains, for his students, whom he calls his children. He says that he wanted them to have in one place what experience had taught him. The earlier parts of the work deal with medicine in general, with drugs and how they are prepared. Surgery comes last.

The final part deals with surgery: how to cauterise with a hot iron, a common treatment of the age, to set broken bones, to treat wounds, to help in difficult births. He describes stitching inside the body with thread made from animal gut. He also complains that the art of surgery had fallen into neglect, because physicians no longer practised it, and that ignorance of anatomy made surgeons dangerous. A surgeon, he warns, must know anatomy thoroughly, must weigh the danger before operating and must never act out of greed.

Drawing the tools was an act of teaching. A student could look at the page and see the shape of the hook, the angle of the blade, the grip of the forceps, and understand exactly what was meant. To a student with no master at hand, a clear drawing was worth a long lecture. The drawings were meant to be used, not admired.

Translated into Latin in the twelfth century, his treatise on surgery was copied, quoted and later printed in Europe, where surgeons relied on it for centuries. Some of the instruments he drew are recognisable in operating theatres today.
lesson: Real masters do not guard their secrets; they explain them so that others can do better. Write down what experience has taught you, and pass it on generously.

title: The Alhambra, the Red Palace of Granada
teaser: The same Arabic motto is carved again and again on a hill above Granada, in a palace built by a small kingdom always under pressure. How did the Nasrids last about two and a half centuries?
story:
On a hill above Granada, the same short Arabic sentence is carved on wall after wall, again and again: There is no victor but God. It was the motto of the Nasrids, the last Muslim dynasty of Spain, and it says a lot about the palace they built.

The Nasrid kingdom was founded in the thirteenth century, at the very time when most of al-Andalus was being lost. Its founder, Muhammad ibn al-Ahmar, made Granada his capital around 1238. The kingdom was small and surrounded by stronger neighbours. It survived by careful diplomacy, by paying tribute to the Christian kings of Castile when necessary, and by the shelter of its mountains. Yet it lasted about two and a half centuries, and on that hill its rulers built the Alhambra — from al-Hamra, the red one, after the colour of its walls.

The Alhambra is really a small walled city: a fortress, royal palaces, houses and gardens, with a summer villa, the Generalife, on the neighbouring hill. From outside it is a plain fortress. Inside, mostly in the fourteenth century, craftsmen created some of the most delicate rooms ever built: carved plaster as fine as lace, coloured tiles in geometric patterns, ceilings like honeycombs, and verses of poetry running along the walls. The plaster was once painted in bright reds, blues and gold, far more colourful than it appears today. Some of those verses were composed by court poets, among them Ibn Zamrak.

Water is everywhere. A canal brought it from the river Darro to the hilltop, and it flows through courtyards, pools and fountains, the most famous of them carried by twelve stone lions. In a dry land, the sound of water and the reflection of arches in a still pool were a luxury, and a reminder of paradise.

Think of the contrast. The fortress stood on its hill as a political world was shrinking around it. Inside, artists carved ornament so refined that it seems made for a calm and secure age. Perhaps that is why the Alhambra moves so many visitors: refined ornament, made with great care, in a kingdom that was always under pressure.

In January 1492, Granada surrendered to the Catholic Monarchs of Spain. The palace survived, and it is today among the most visited monuments in Spain.
lesson: Beauty does not need size or power; it needs care and humility. Even in an uncertain time, you can make something fine that will outlast your worries.

title: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: Power as a Trust
teaser: In 717 a man learned he now ruled an empire from Spain to Central Asia; tradition relates he took it as a burden, not a prize. What did he do with that power in barely more than two years?
story:
In 717, a man learns that he has just been named ruler of an empire stretching from Spain to Central Asia. Tradition relates that he received the news as a burden, not a prize.

Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz was a prince of the Umayyad family, raised in comfort, and through his mother a great-grandson of the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab. Before becoming caliph he had served as governor of Medina, where he was known for his interest in scholars. His predecessor, Sulayman, had named him in his will, to the surprise of many. The empire was home to many peoples, and more of them were becoming Muslim every year, which raised hard questions about fairness. Once caliph, the accounts agree, he changed his way of life. He gave up luxury and handed over to the public treasury wealth that he judged his family had no right to keep; tradition adds that his wife Fatima gave up her jewels too.

He listened to complaints against governors and removed those who were unjust. He lightened unfair taxes. Accounts of his reign also stress that he wanted new Muslims treated fairly, and that he did not want converts to be burdened with the taxes that had been paid by non-Muslims. And he called back the army that had spent a year besieging Constantinople, a campaign that had cost the Muslims dearly.

He also wrote to scholars asking them to gather the sayings of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in writing, for fear that knowledge would disappear with those who carried it — an important step in the history of hadith collection. Among those who answered the call was the scholar Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri.

Later writers relate that in some provinces, the officials in charge of charity struggled to find anyone poor enough to receive it. Whether or not every detail is exact, the story shows what people remembered about his reign: a time when the treasury was treated as a trust.

He died in 720, not yet forty, after little more than two years in power. Muslims have remembered him ever since as a model of the just ruler. His reign was too short to know what more he might have done.
lesson: Authority is a responsibility to carry, not a privilege to enjoy. Wherever you are in charge, at home, at school or at work, begin by being strict with yourself.

title: Al-Jazari and His Ingenious Machines
teaser: An elephant carries a tower on its back; at intervals a bird whistles, a serpent tips forward and the driver moves. It is a water clock designed over eight hundred years ago: how did it work?
story:
An elephant carries a tower on its back. At regular intervals the figures on it come to life: a bird whistles, a serpent tips forward, the elephant's driver moves. It is a clock, driven by water, and it was designed more than eight hundred years ago. Whoever built it had to understand weight, flow and balance.

Its inventor, al-Jazari, was an engineer at the court of the Artuqid princes in Diyar Bakr, in what is now south-eastern Turkey, where he served for about twenty-five years. His family had served the court before him. In 1206, at the request of his ruler, Nasir al-Din Mahmud, he completed a book describing about fifty machines: clocks, fountains, vessels that pour drinks by themselves, devices for washing hands and machines for raising water.

The inside of the elephant clock works like this. A bowl with a small hole floats in a tank of water. As the bowl slowly fills and sinks, it pulls on cords connected to the figures above. Water, falling at an even rate, becomes a way of measuring time and of setting a mechanism in motion at the right moment.

He arranges the machines in six categories, from clocks and drinking vessels to fountains and water-raising machines. Two things make the book exceptional. First, the mechanisms: one of his water-raising machines uses a crank and connecting rod to turn rotation into back-and-forth movement, a principle found today in car engines. Second, his method. He explains that he describes only what he has built and tested himself, and he gives measurements and drawings so that other craftsmen can build the machines in turn.

In his description, the elephant, the dragons and the phoenix recall the cultures of India, China and Egypt. Not every machine is practical. Some were made for pleasure, such as the fountains and the automatic servants at a prince's table. But they show a taste for understanding how things work, and for turning understanding into a working object.

Manuscripts of the book, with colourful paintings of the machines, survive in several museums. Several of his devices have been rebuilt in modern times by following his descriptions, and they work. The proof of a good explanation is that someone else, centuries later, can make the thing again.
lesson: An idea is only finished when it has been built and tested. Do not just imagine: make it, check that it works, and explain it clearly enough for others to repeat.

title: How Islam Sailed to the Malay World
teaser: Islam did not first reach Southeast Asia's islands with an army but with merchants, on winds that blow one way for months, then the other. How did a faith carried by traders take root from Sumatra to Java?
story:
Islam did not first reach the islands of Southeast Asia with an army. It came by ship, with merchants, on the monsoon winds.

Those winds shaped everything. For months they blow from one direction, and then from the other. A ship that left India for the Strait of Malacca had to wait in port for the wind to change before it could sail home. Traders therefore spent long seasons in foreign harbours. Marco Polo, passing through in 1292, noted that one port on Sumatra already followed the law of Muhammad, while its neighbours did not. For centuries, merchants from Arabia, Persia and India had sailed to the ports of Sumatra, Malaya and Java in search of spices, on the sea route to China. Many were Muslims. They settled in the harbour towns, married there and built mosques; scholars and Sufi teachers followed. Little by little, local rulers adopted the faith of their trading partners.

In northern Sumatra, the gravestone of Sultan Malik al-Salih, ruler of the port of Samudra-Pasai, bears the date 1297: it is one of the oldest traces of a Muslim kingdom in the region. The sultans of Pasai later struck coins with Arabic inscriptions. A Malay chronicle written later wraps his story in legend. When Ibn Battuta stopped there half a century later, he found a sultan who loved discussing religious law with scholars.

In the fifteenth century the rulers of Malacca, a new port on the strait between Malaya and Sumatra, became Muslim as well. Malacca grew into one of the busiest harbours in the world, where ships met from India, China and the islands. Its language, Malay, written in Arabic letters, helped carry the faith from island to island, and became a common language for trade and learning across the archipelago. Malacca fell to the Portuguese in 1511, but by then the faith was firmly rooted.

In Java, tradition remembers nine saints, the wali songo, who are said to have taught the faith gently. The details are wrapped in legend, but the memory shows how people understood the spread of Islam: as the work of teachers and neighbours rather than of conquerors.

Today, Indonesia and Malaysia together are home to well over two hundred million Muslims.
lesson: People are convinced by how you behave long before they listen to what you say. Honest dealing in everyday life is the most powerful message you can carry.

title: The Bimaristan: A Hospital Open to All
teaser: In Cairo in 1284 a hospital opened its doors to everyone: rich and poor, men and women, slaves and strangers, without payment. Who paid for it, and how could it keep going for centuries?
story:
Cairo, 1284. A new hospital opens its doors, and its founding charter sets out who may be treated there: everyone. Rich and poor, men and women, free people and slaves, residents and strangers, without payment. Qalawun, a Mamluk sultan who had come to power in 1279, wanted it to serve the whole city.

It was built by Sultan Qalawun and known as the Mansuri hospital. It stood in the heart of the city, as part of a great complex that also included a mosque, a school and the sultan's tomb. Tradition relates that Qalawun himself had once been treated in the Nuri hospital in Damascus and had been so impressed that he vowed to build a hospital worthy of it.

Inside, men and women had separate wards. There were sections for different conditions: fevers, eye diseases, wounds, stomach illnesses and mental illness. There was a pharmacy, kitchens and a place for teaching medicine. The great physician Ibn al-Nafis, who worked in Cairo in those years, left it his library. The sultan's endowment deed named the shops, houses and lands whose income would pay for the staff, the medicines and the food.

Such a hospital was called a bimaristan, from a Persian word meaning place of the sick. The first were founded in Baghdad from about the year 800, and others followed in Damascus, in Cairo, and from Anatolia to al-Andalus. Doctors made their rounds with their students, and learned at the bedside. Standards mattered: in Baghdad in 931, after a patient died through a physician's error, the caliph ordered that doctors be examined before they were allowed to practise.

How was all this paid for, with free care? Through the waqf: a founder gave property — shops, land, baths — whose income was reserved for the hospital for ever. It could not be sold or inherited. The gift went on working long after the giver had died. A hospital of this kind was not a business, and not a favour: it was a public service, financed by the generosity of one man and administered by trustees.

The Mansuri hospital cared for patients for centuries, and the great complex of Qalawun, with its mosque, school and tomb, still stands in Cairo. In a time when many people lived far from a doctor, a door that was always open was a rare gift.
lesson: The best generosity is organised to last. When you want to do good, think about how it can keep working after the first enthusiasm, and even after you.

title: Mus'ab ibn Umayr, the First Envoy
period: Dawn of Islam, Mecca and Medina
teaser: The early biographies relate that the best-dressed young man in Mecca accepted Islam, and his furious mother cut him off from the family's wealth. Why did the Prophet ﷺ send him to a divided city?
story:
In Mecca, everyone knew Mus'ab ibn Umayr: the young man from a wealthy family, with the finest clothes and perfume. Then he accepted Islam. The early biographies relate that his mother, furious, shut him in and cut him off from the family's wealth. He chose his faith, and a much poorer life.

Meanwhile, the oasis of Yathrib, several days' journey to the north, was a troubled place. Its two great Arab tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj, had fought each other for years, and the exhausted city was looking for a way to live in peace. Around the year 621, a small group from Yathrib — the oasis that would soon be called Medina — pledged themselves to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ sent Mus'ab back with them to teach them the Qur'an. He was the first envoy of Islam.

It was a delicate mission. He was a stranger in a divided city, and he came with no army and no wealth. In Yathrib he stayed with As'ad ibn Zurara and taught patiently.

Then came the test. Two clan leaders, Usayd ibn Hudayr and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, came one after the other intending to stop him. He invited each to sit and listen first. Both accepted Islam, and many of their people followed.

A year later, more than seventy men and women from Yathrib came to Mecca to pledge their support to the Prophet ﷺ. The city was ready to welcome him. Soon after, the migration to Medina began.

At Uhud, a mountain just north of Medina, the Muslims faced a Meccan army that had come to avenge its defeat at Badr the year before. Mus'ab was killed there in 625, carrying the Muslims' banner. His companions related that the only cloth they had for his shroud was too short to cover him completely: if they covered his head, his feet were bare. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have had them cover his head with the cloth and put fragrant grass on his feet. The man who had once worn the finest clothes in Mecca left the world with almost nothing, and the city he had taught became the home of Islam.
lesson: Gentleness opens doors that force cannot. When someone comes to you angry, invite them to sit and listen first; patience and good manners are often the strongest argument.

title: Al-Biruni Measures the Earth From a Mountain
period: Ghaznavid Empire, Central Asia and India
teaser: On a height in what is now Pakistan, a scholar aims an instrument at the horizon, meaning to measure the whole Earth with one mountain and some geometry. How can a tiny angle reveal the size of a planet?
story:
On a height near the fort of Nandana, in what is now Pakistan, a scholar aims his instrument at the horizon. With one mountain and some geometry, he intends to measure the whole Earth.

Abu Rayhan al-Biruni was born in 973 in Khwarazm, in Central Asia. In the early eleventh century he came to India in the wake of the armies of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni. While others looked for treasure, he looked for knowledge: he studied Sanskrit, talked with Indian scholars and wrote a large, fair-minded book, the Kitab al-Hind, describing India's sciences, beliefs and customs. He tried to present what Indians themselves believed and wrote, and not what outsiders said about them.

His idea at Nandana was elegant. First he measured the height of the mountain, by taking two sightings of its summit from two points on the plain. Then, from its top, he measured how far the horizon dipped below a level line. That angle is tiny, a fraction of a degree. But from that small angle and the mountain's height, trigonometry gave him the radius of the Earth. Why did it matter? To find the distance between two cities, or the direction of Mecca from a distant land, a geographer needs to know how big the Earth is. Al-Biruni cared about such questions, and he recorded his method in his astronomical writings.

Converted into modern units, his result is usually reckoned to be within about one or two per cent of today's value, though the exact length of his unit is uncertain.

It was a bold shortcut. About two centuries earlier, scholars working for the caliph al-Ma'mun had measured the Earth by having teams measure out long distances across the plains of Iraq. Al-Biruni's method needed only a mountain, an instrument and careful observation. Scholars of his time had inherited Greek geometry and trigonometry and developed both further, and his method rests on that tradition.

He was a scholar of many interests, writing on astronomy, mathematics, geography, medicine, minerals and history. He left behind well over a hundred works, most of them now lost. He is said to have kept working into old age, and he died around 1048.
lesson: A good method is worth more than great resources. Before saying a task is too big for you, look for the clever angle from which it becomes possible.

title: Sinan, the Architect Who Kept Learning
teaser: He was about fifty when he became chief architect of the Ottoman Empire, an age when many careers wind down. His lasted another half-century: which of his works is said to be his masterpiece?
story:
He was about fifty when he was named chief architect of the Ottoman Empire, an age at which many careers are winding down. His would last another half-century.

Sinan was born around 1490 in a Christian village of central Anatolia. As a young man he was recruited into the sultan's service, became a Muslim and joined the Janissaries. On campaign from the Balkans to Iraq, he learned his craft the hard way, building bridges, fortifications and ships as a military engineer. Armies cannot wait for perfect plans: a bridge must carry the soldiers across the river, and it must be ready in time.

In 1539 Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent put him in charge of imperial building, at the head of a large office of masons, carpenters, engineers and draughtsmen. Sinan served three sultans, and the lists of his works drawn up in his own time count more than three hundred: mosques, schools, hospitals, baths, bridges, aqueducts. The great bridge over the Drina at Visegrad, in Bosnia, is credited to him. He also helped to reinforce Hagia Sophia with new buttresses.

Hagia Sophia, the great domed church of the Byzantines, by then a mosque, was the model that every Ottoman architect had to face. Sinan spent his career exploring how to cover a vast hall with a dome, so that the whole space could be seen at once, light and open. He tried different supports and different shapes in building after building.

He never stopped trying to do better. A saying long attributed to him calls the Şehzade Mosque in Istanbul the work of his apprenticeship, the Süleymaniye that of his journeyman years, and the Selimiye in Edirne, finished when he was in his eighties, his masterpiece.

The Selimiye's great dome rests on eight pillars above a hall flooded with light. The Süleymaniye, finished in 1557, is not only a mosque: its complex also held schools, a hospital, baths and a soup kitchen. Among Sinan's apprentices was Mehmed Agha, who later built the Blue Mosque of Istanbul. The Selimiye was built for Sultan Selim II between 1568 and 1574. Sinan died in 1588 and rests in a modest tomb he designed himself, beside the Süleymaniye. His buildings still mark the skylines of Istanbul, Edirne and many other towns.
lesson: It is never too late to begin, and never time to stop improving. Treat each thing you finish as a lesson for the next one.

title: Timbuktu, the City That Treasured Books
period: Mali and Songhai empires, West Africa
teaser: In sixteenth-century Timbuktu a visitor noted that handwritten books earned more profit than any other goods in the market. What did the people of the city do with them when armed conflict arrived in 2012?
story:
In sixteenth-century Timbuktu, on the southern edge of the Sahara, a visitor noted something that surprised him: among all the goods sold in the market, handwritten books brought in more profit than any other merchandise.

That visitor is known as Leo Africanus, and the city he described was at its height. Enriched by the trade in gold and salt, Timbuktu had become, under the Mali and then the Songhai empires, a city of scholars. The Songhai ruler Askia Muhammad, who had made the pilgrimage to Mecca in the 1490s, honoured learned men. Caravans from the north brought salt, and boats on the Niger brought goods from the south. Students came from elsewhere in West Africa to study. Around the mosques of the city, especially Sankore, teachers gave lessons in law, grammar, astronomy and medicine.

Books were imported across the desert, copied by hand and commented on by local authors, in Arabic and sometimes in African languages written in Arabic script. The most famous of these scholars, Ahmad Baba, who died in 1627, said that his library of about 1,600 volumes was smaller than those of others in his family. He had paid a price for his learning: after Morocco conquered the region in 1591, he was taken to Marrakesh, and returned to Timbuktu only years later.

The books survived because families kept them, generation after generation, in chests and in the rooms of old houses. The climate of the desert edge helped: dry air is kind to paper. Each family guarded its inheritance, and passed it from father to child. The manuscripts deal with religion, but also with astronomy, medicine, mathematics and poetry, and even with business contracts and letters. Timbuktu's old mosques and its tombs are today a World Heritage Site.

In 2012, when armed conflict reached the city, librarians and ordinary residents secretly carried a very large part of the manuscripts to safety, trunk by trunk. Estimates of the number of manuscripts held in the region run into the hundreds of thousands. They were moved in secret, hidden in houses, and carried south by road and river.

Timbuktu had grown rich on gold and salt. What its people chose to save, when danger came, was their books.
lesson: A community shows what it truly values by what it protects in hard times. Take care of books and of the knowledge handed down to you; they are an inheritance for those who come after.

title: Al-Idrisi Maps the World for a King
teaser: In Palermo in the 1140s, a Muslim scholar at a Christian king's court questions travellers and keeps only what the witnesses agree on. Could a map of the whole world be built from other people's eyes?
story:
Palermo, Sicily, in the 1140s. At the court of a Christian king, a Muslim scholar is gathering reports from travellers: where they have been, how many days separate one town from the next, what grows there and what is sold. The accounts are compared, and what the witnesses agree on is kept; what they contradict is set aside.

The king is Roger II, a Norman ruler. Sicily had been ruled by Muslims since the ninth century before the Normans conquered it in the eleventh. His island is home to Latin and Greek Christians, Muslims and Jews. His court is a place where Arabic, Greek and Latin are all heard, and where Arab craftsmen and scholars still work. The scholar is al-Idrisi, born around 1100 in Ceuta, on the coast of North Africa. He had studied in Cordoba and travelled in Spain and North Africa before coming to Sicily. Roger, a patron of learning, has asked him for nothing less than a description of the whole known world.

It was an enormous task. Al-Idrisi drew on the writings of earlier geographers, Greek and Muslim, and on the accounts of merchants, sailors and pilgrims who came to Palermo. Where they disagreed, he weighed their words. He was building a picture of the world out of other people's eyes.

The work took about fifteen years. It was completed in 1154, shortly before the king died. It is a great book of geography, often called the Book of Roger, which divides the world into seventy sections, each with its own map, from the Atlantic to China, seven climate zones of ten sections each, with notes on distances, products and customs. The maps place south at the top, as was common among Muslim mapmakers, so that Africa appears above Europe. They are schematic, not like modern maps, but they are rich in names, routes and distances.

Al-Idrisi also had a large map of the world engraved on silver, which has since been lost. He later wrote another geographical work for Roger's son, William I.

For a long time his work remained one of the most detailed descriptions of the world ever made. It was born of a simple method: ask, compare, verify.
lesson: Before repeating something, check it against more than one source. Reliable knowledge is built by asking, comparing and keeping only what holds up.

title: Ibn al-Nafis and the Path of the Blood
period: Ayyubid and Mamluk Syria and Egypt
teaser: In 1924 a young Egyptian doctor in Germany opened an old Arabic manuscript and found a discovery that history books credited to Europeans three centuries later. What had its author understood about the heart?
story:
In 1924, a young Egyptian doctor studying in Germany examined an old Arabic manuscript kept in Berlin, and found in it a discovery that the history books credited to Europeans of three centuries later. His name was Muhyi al-Din al-Tatawi, and he was preparing a study of Ibn al-Nafis at the University of Freiburg.

The author was Ibn al-Nafis. Born near Damascus around 1213, he studied medicine at the city's Nuri hospital and then settled in Cairo, where he became chief physician of Egypt. He is also said to have served as physician to the Mamluk sultan Baybars. Around 1242 he wrote a commentary on the anatomy in Ibn Sina's Canon, a book every doctor knew.

The problem he tackled was ancient. For more than a thousand years, doctors had followed the Greek physician Galen, who taught that blood passed from the right side of the heart to the left through invisible pores in the wall between them. Ibn Sina and others had repeated the idea. Ibn al-Nafis argued plainly that there are no such pores: the wall is solid.

If the blood cannot pass through the wall, where does it go? Blood from the right side, he wrote, must travel to the lungs, mix there with air, and return to the left side of the heart. He had described the circulation of blood through the lungs. He also wrote that the heart is nourished by the vessels that run over its surface, and not by the blood inside its chambers.

His insight seems to have been little noticed in his own time. In Europe, the circulation through the lungs was described again in the sixteenth century, by physicians such as Michael Servetus and Realdo Colombo, and in the following century William Harvey described the circulation of the blood through the whole body.

Ibn al-Nafis kept working and writing until his death in Cairo in 1288, and left his house and his books to the new Mansuri hospital. It took the eyes of a student, nearly seven centuries later, to bring his page back into the light.
lesson: Respecting your teachers does not mean repeating their mistakes. Say what the evidence shows, calmly and honestly, even if recognition comes late or never.

title: The Astrolabe-Maker of Aleppo
teaser: Nearly everything known about her fits in one line of a tenth-century book, and we are not even sure of her first name. Who was the woman who made astrolabes at the court of Aleppo?
story:
We do not know her first name for certain. We do not know when she was born or when she died. Nearly everything known about her fits in one line of a tenth-century book, and yet she has not been forgotten.

Around 987, a Baghdad bookseller named Ibn al-Nadim compiled a great catalogue of the books and scholars of his time. In his list of the makers of astrolabes he mentions a woman: al-Ijliya, daughter of the astrolabe-maker al-Ijli, who had trained under a master of the craft and worked at the court of Sayf al-Dawla, ruler of Aleppo in Syria from about 944 to 967. That is all. The name Mariam, by which she is widely known today, does not appear in that text, and none of her instruments is known to survive.

But the line says a lot. Sayf al-Dawla's court was famous for its poets and scholars, and to be employed there was an honour. Aleppo in those years was also a frontier city, defended by its ruler against the Byzantines, and a meeting place of poets such as al-Mutanabbi and of the philosopher al-Farabi. And an astrolabe was a precision tool: a brass disc engraved with a map of the sky, hung from a ring so that the user could hold it up and sight a star along its back, used to tell the time, find the direction of Mecca and measure the height of the stars. For a Muslim city, it answered practical questions: when is the hour of prayer, and in which direction should the believer face?

Think of what it took to make one. The craftsman had to calculate the lines for a given latitude, engrave them with a steady hand on a thin plate, and fit together several moving parts so that they turned smoothly. A small error could make the whole instrument useless. Making one required mathematics, astronomy and a skilled engraver's hand.

She did not invent it, as is sometimes claimed; it is far older. Her place in history is more modest, and more human: she was a woman who practised a demanding craft, and was good enough to work for a prince.

The single line that remembers her has done its work. Today, an asteroid bears her name.
lesson: Honesty about what we do not know is part of respecting the past. And remember that good work matters even when history keeps only one line about the person who did it.

title: Salah ad-Din Enters Jerusalem Without a Massacre
teaser: In October 1187 the people of Jerusalem remembered the massacre of 1099, and now Saladin's army stood at their walls. Would history repeat itself?
story:
October 1187. Inside the walls of Jerusalem, people are terrified. They remember what happened when the Crusaders took the city in 1099: its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants were massacred. Now the army of Salah ad-Din — Saladin, a name that means righteousness of the faith — surrounds them, and they expect the same.

The city is crowded. Refugees from the surrounding country have poured in, and few trained soldiers remain: much of the Crusader army had been destroyed at Hattin three months earlier. Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, had spent years uniting those lands under his rule, and he had won that battle. His men besieged Jerusalem from the end of September and undermined a section of the northern wall. After a short siege, the city's defender, Balian of Ibelin, came out to negotiate.

The agreement reached was that the city would surrender without bloodshed, and that its inhabitants could buy their freedom for a fixed ransom and leave in safety. The Muslim chronicles give the sums as ten dinars for a man, five for a woman and one for a child.

On 2 October, Saladin's troops entered Jerusalem. There was no massacre. According to the chroniclers, Saladin posted guards to keep order in the streets and at the gates, and guards protected the departing columns on the road. The arrangement was not gentle for everyone: many who could not pay were taken into captivity, as was the custom of the age. But chroniclers on both sides record that Saladin and his brother freed large numbers of the poor without payment, the elderly among them.

The city's Muslim life resumed. The first Friday prayer in the al-Aqsa Mosque was held about a week later. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre was left standing, and Eastern Christians remained in the city.

The fall of the city shocked Europe and led to the Third Crusade, which did not recover Jerusalem. Even there, Saladin was long remembered as a chivalrous enemy who kept his word. Chroniclers relate that when he died in Damascus in 1193 he had given away so much that little was left in his treasury. The memory of that autumn shows that mercy was possible even after decades of bitter war.
lesson: Strength shows its true quality at the moment of victory. When you have the upper hand, keep your word and choose mercy over revenge.

title: The Taj Mahal: Grief Turned Into Marble
teaser: In 1631 an emperor lost his wife far from home, and the next year work began on her tomb. How did its builders make verses high on a wall look the same size from the ground?
story:
In 1631, in the middle of a military campaign, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan lost his wife. Mumtaz Mahal, whose name means the chosen one of the palace, died giving birth to their fourteenth child. She was first buried at Burhanpur, and her body was later moved to Agra. The court chroniclers describe an emperor overcome by grief. She had accompanied him even on campaign, and her death came far from home.

The following year, on the bank of the river Yamuna at Agra, in northern India, work began on her tomb. Thousands of craftsmen and labourers took part. White marble was brought from Makrana, in Rajasthan, hundreds of kilometres away, and other stones came from farther still to be set into the walls. The main building rose in about a decade, and the whole complex, with its mosque, gateway and gardens, was complete by about 1653.

Everything in it is balance, and the white marble seems to change colour with the light of the day. The tomb rises from a platform with a slender minaret at each corner. The complex is today a World Heritage Site. The tomb stands at the end of a long garden divided by water channels, an image of the gardens of Paradise. You pass through a great gateway, and suddenly the white dome appears, framed by the arch. Verses of the Qur'an frame the great arches, designed by the calligrapher Amanat Khan.

He solved a subtle problem. Letters high on a wall look smaller from below. So the letters grow larger as they climb, so that from the ground they all seem the same size. Flowers of coloured stone are set into the marble, each petal cut and fitted by hand.

The architect of the whole is traditionally said to be Ustad Ahmad Lahori, though many hands shaped it. In his later years Shah Jahan was deposed by his son Aurangzeb and kept at Agra Fort, within sight of the tomb, it is said.

Shah Jahan died in 1666 and was buried beside his wife. The popular tale that the workers' hands were cut off so that they could never build its equal has no historical basis.
lesson: Sorrow can be turned into something that gives beauty to others. And before repeating a dramatic story, ask whether it is actually true.

title: Ibn Khaldun and the Science of Societies
teaser: In 1375 a tired statesman who had known both favour and prison shut himself in a small fortress in what is now Algeria to ask why kingdoms rise and fall. What answer did he find?
story:
In 1375, a tired statesman shut himself away in a small fortress in the countryside of what is now Algeria. He had served several courts, and had known both favour and prison. A tribe of the region sheltered him there for about four years. Now he wanted to understand: why do kingdoms rise, and why do they fall?

Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in 1332, into a family of Andalusian origin. As a teenager he lost his parents and several of his teachers to the Black Death. For some twenty years he lived the dangerous life of a court official, from Fez to Granada. He saw ministers fall overnight, rulers deposed or killed, and fortunes reversed. He spent time in prison himself.

In the fortress of Ibn Salama he began a history of the world, and completed the first draft of its introduction, the Muqaddima, in 1377. In it he asks historians to stop repeating tales and to check whether what they report is even possible. He studies how climate, work, trade, taxes and education shape societies. A ruler who raises taxes too high, he argues, discourages work and ends up with less. The introduction opens a larger history of the Arabs, the Berbers and their neighbours.

And he describes a force he calls asabiyya, the solidarity that binds a group together: strong among those who live a hard life, it lets them build a state, then fades with comfort, generation after generation. He reckoned that a dynasty rarely lasted much beyond three generations.

The scholar later settled in Cairo, where he taught and served several times as a judge, being dismissed and reappointed more than once. He tells that in 1401, when the conqueror Timur besieged Damascus, he was lowered by ropes over the city wall to meet him.

He kept revising the Muqaddima for years, and in his later years he wrote an autobiography. He argued that history should look not only at kings and battles but at how people make a living. He died in Cairo in 1406. Many see in him a forerunner of sociology and economics, a man who turned his own hard experience into a way of understanding history.
lesson: Step back from events to look for their causes. Whoever understands why things happen, instead of only what happened, is better prepared for what comes next.
